lazarus.title: Is the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) a warning about hell?
lazarus.summary: Myers argues the story is the last of five parables answering the Pharisees' complaint in Luke 15:1-2, and its target is greed. The rich man stands for the money-loving religious leaders of Luke 16:14. His flames are no more literal than Abraham's bosom: they picture the agony of a thirsty soul and the painful revelation of who he really is. The great gulf is a divide of his own making, a picture of humanly created alienation rather than medieval hell.
points: Read as a lesson on escaping hell, the story would teach that heaven is earned by being poor or generous to the poor, which contradicts eternal life as a free gift received by believing.
Abraham's bosom comes from Babylonian-influenced Jewish tales of one afterlife with two regions. Jesus used it the way someone today might tell a story about Peter at the Pearly Gates.
Elsewhere Jesus uses hades only for the destruction of cities; for individuals in hell he says gehenna. Here he mixes Greek, Babylonian and Jewish imagery to make a memorable story.
The story inverts the Prodigal Son: both beggars crave scraps beside unclean animals and lean on a father figure, but the prodigal comes to his senses while the rich man never changes.
Lazarus at the gate may echo gate proselytes, Gentile converts kept outside the inner courts who longed to draw near to God but were held at a distance by the religious leaders.
Odunomai, tormented, appears elsewhere only in Luke 2:48 for the anxiety of Mary and Joseph and Acts 20:38 for the Ephesian elders' sorrow: emotional anguish, not torture.
Even in Hades the rich man orders Lazarus around and never speaks to him, yet Abraham calls him son. He will not cross the chasm because he cannot admit he is no better than Lazarus.
lazarus.differs: The topic treats basanos as a purifying touchstone test and the chasm as the Jordan Rift Valley. Myers reads the touchstone as unmasking the rich man and the chasm as a social divide he himself created.

quote.text: Money satisfies those who chase after it less than a drop of water on the tongue would satisfy a man who is burning in flames.

richfool.title: Does Mark 9:42-50 teach about hell when it refers to worms and fire?
richfool.summary: Myers argues that the worm and fire of Mark 9 are not the torment of the dead but the self-inflicted corruption and destruction of sin, drawn from Isaiah 66:24. Being salted with fire describes the self-sacrifice, loving discipline and fiery trials that purify disciples in this life. Jesus urges them to keep their lives free of corruption now, not so they can escape hell, but so they experience God's reign here and avoid the ruin sin brings.
points: The worm, skolex, feeds on dead bodies, not living ones burning in flames. Since worms and fire cannot both be literal, both must be symbolic, as Gehenna's corpses once were.
Throughout Isaiah, fire and worms picture destruction and corruption that come on rebels, often self-inflicted. That is why Isaiah speaks of their worm: they brought it on themselves.
In Isaiah 66:24 the redeemed look on the corpse of human history, including their own failures. This knowledge of evil, which Adam and Eve lacked, keeps them from rebelling again.
If the fire in 'everyone will be salted with fire' meant hell, Jesus would be sending everyone there. Salt preserved meat from worms, so purifying fire and salt stop destruction and decay.
Jesus equates salt with peace with one another. Since destruction often comes through wars, being seasoned for peace is a primary way to avert human violence.
Following William Lane, every disciple is a sacrifice salted like temple offerings in Leviticus 2:13, seasoned through fiery trials, a call to living self-sacrifice as in Romans 12:1.
richfool.differs: The topic notes readers disagree whether the worm and fire picture endless torment or total destruction. Myers rejects both: they describe the self-inflicted corruption of sin now, and Isaiah's corpses are the remembered history of all humanity.

quote.text: Eternity will not be much of a blessed existence if we cannot remember what God redeemed us from.

sheepgoats.title: Is the everlasting fire of Matthew 25:41 a warning about hell?
sheepgoats.summary: Myers reads the Sheep and the Goats as the climax of three parables contrasting the kingdom of God with the kingdom of this world. The everlasting fire is not torture in hell but the refining discipline that falls on nations whose people neglect the poor, echoing Ezekiel's judgments on Sodom and Israel. It is everlasting because it comes from the everlasting God, and the nations are eventually restored. The parable reveals that Jesus dwells among the least of these.
points: The Olivet Discourse answers the disciples' questions about the temple's fall and the end of the age, fulfilled within one generation when Rome razed Jerusalem less than forty years later.
Kolasis, punishment, originally meant cut short, with pruning in the background according to Moulton-Milligan. Its only other New Testament use is 1 John 4:18, where love casts out fear.
In the Septuagint, kolasis appears in Ezekiel 14, and Ezekiel 16:49 says Sodom's sin was not helping the poor. Ezekiel even calls such nations' ruin everlasting desolation, yet promises restoration.
The devil means accuser. His angels are the principalities guiding the nations, and the fire prepared for them is discipline teaching nations to live as God wants.
Debates over who the nations and the least of these are let readers miss the point. Limiting care to one group or era makes a person self-identify as a goat.
God has been hiding among the poor, sick, weak and hungry all along. To see God, Jesus says, go serve the poor, for that is where he lives.
sheepgoats.differs: The topic reads the goats as Israel's selfish leaders and verse 46 as age-long correction. Myers applies it to every nation's people, defining kolasis as pruning and the fire as God's refining discipline of nations.

quote.text: True service to your country does not look like marching off to war to kill others, but instead looks like feeding the hungry and clothing the poor that are in our midst.

unquenchable.title: Does the unquenchable fire of Matthew 3:10-12 refer to hell?
unquenchable.summary: Myers argues that John the Baptist is warning of imminent temporal judgment on Israel, fulfilled when Rome burned Jerusalem in 69-70 AD, not of hell or annihilation. The axe, the burning trees, the baptism of fire and the chaff all picture the nation's destruction if it does not repent. Unquenchable fire simply burns until its task is complete. John invites his hearers to burn the rubbish out of their lives now, or have it burned later when the Messiah comes.
points: Modern teachers use these verses to argue true Christians must prove themselves by works or face hell. That misuse comes from assuming the fire means hell.
The root of the tree is Israel's ruling class, the source of its teaching; the tree is the rest of the nation, following Keener. Both face being cut down without repentance.
Baptism means immersion, so immersion in fire is consumption by fire. Jesus does not send it; the destruction comes through Israel's rejection of him as Messiah.
Asbestos also named quicklime from ancient kilns, which resembles the ash of a completely burned body, as Isaiah 33:12 pictures.
Jeremiah 17:27 promised an unquenchable fire on Jerusalem's gates. Nebuchadnezzar burned the city in 586 BC, yet the fire burned out and the city was later rebuilt.
Repentance is not a condition for eternal life, received by believing in Jesus, but a real turning from sin. Those who refuse experience their choices' destructive consequences.
unquenchable.differs: The topic stresses fire as purifying the chaff within each person. Myers reads John's fire chiefly as the national destruction of Israel in 69-70 AD, though he adds that unrepentant Israel met fires of purification.

quote.text: He invites his listeners to burn the rubbish out of their own lives now in preparation for the Messiah, or have it burned up later when the Messiah comes.

destruction.title: Does 2 Thessalonians 1:8-9 teach about hell?
destruction.summary: Myers calls this possibly the strongest text for eternal torment, yet argues it describes the ruin in this life of the plans of people and nations who oppose God. Tribulation, flaming fire and everlasting destruction are three parallel phrases for temporal consequences. Destruction comes from neglecting God's honor, not from God: sin carries its own penalty. Everlasting destruction means plans ruined beyond repair, neither annihilation nor ongoing torture, and their work fades from memory with no lasting significance.
points: Isaiah 2 speaks of the terror of the Lord, but Paul removes terror and inserts the presence of the Lord. Myers calls this change significant.
The preposition from is causal, but God is not the cause. Humans who despise the Lord's honor bring destruction on themselves by ignoring instructions given for their good.
Punished, diken tisousin, is better rendered pay the penalty, like a player sent to the penalty box. The player is not punished but pays the price of his choice.
Olethron means ruin. A dropped meal still exists but can never be eaten; it is eternally ruined because it cannot be salvaged, not because the ruining continues.

In the Septuagint, olethros mostly describes foreign nations plotting against Israel whose own plans come to nothing. The people may live on, some even Christians, but their plans have no eternal significance.
This ruin can come in history, as with Jerusalem and Rome, or at the Judgment Seat of Christ, when believers see their wood, hay and stubble burned up.
destruction.differs: The topic says a literal reading would point to annihilation. Myers denies it means either annihilation or torment, and says the consequences come from neglecting God's honor, not from God himself.

quote.text: For those of us who want to be remembered and to make an impact on this world, this is a dire warning indeed.

vine.title: Do the warning passages of Hebrews 6:7-8 and Hebrews 10:27 refer to Christians going to hell?
vine.summary: Myers argues that the land in Hebrews 6:7-8 is the lives of Christians, so a hell reading would mean Christians can be damned. Instead, three parallel terms, rejected, cursed and burned, describe God declaring an unfruitful believer's life useless and burning over the field so it can be plowed and planted again. The passage is about the restorative discipline God gives his own children, and so actually affirms eternal security.
points: Hebrews has five warning passages; the one in chapter 6 is both the most severely worded and the most widely misunderstood.
Adokimos, rejected, means disapproved or useless, not lacking eternal life. Esau in Hebrews 12:17 lost his earthly blessing and was rejected despite tears.
The thorns and briers are the cares, riches and pleasures of this world that choke the seed, as in the parable of the sower in Luke 8.
Cursed, katara, is a verbal declaration, the opposite of the blessing, eulogia, which means verbal praise. It declares the field useless rather than describing an action.
Kausis, burning, appears only here; its verb is used in 2 Peter 3:10. Farmers burn thorny fields to prepare them for plowing, a correction that leaves the soil intact.
In Hebrews 10:27 the fiery indignation is not God's but a sinful human zeal that consumes those who reject God's love and live in fear of him.
vine.differs: The topic notes one commentator who calls field-burning remedial. Myers makes that the whole point: the burning is God's loving discipline of believers, as Hebrews 12:6 says, not destruction or damnation.

quote.text: This passage is not talking about Christians who lose their eternal life and end up in hell.

jude.title: Will Licentiousness and Lewdness send you to hell? (Jude 4, Jude 7)
jude.summary: Myers says the false teachers of Jude 4 taught that grace is a license to sin without serious consequences. Eternal security, rightly taught, says grace allows sin but also teaches that sin brings real devastation. The eternal fire of Jude 7 is the visible, lasting destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, not hell: a penalty their own actions brought on them. Abusing grace invites fire into a person's life, leaving only dust and ashes.
points: Grace that is restricted to prevent abuse is no longer grace. True grace by definition opens itself to abuse, yet when understood it teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11-12 says.
Jude gives three parallel examples. The wilderness Israelites died physically; the angels sit in chains and darkness, not fire, since darkness and fire are mutually exclusive.
Sodom was set forth as an example people could see. A hidden future punishment in hellfire could not serve as a visible historical example to humanity.
Jude 23 speaks of pulling people out of the fire, as Lot was rescued from Sodom. Few traditionalists would say people can be rescued from hell once there.
Dikēn hupechousai means to undergo justice. Jude 10 says the false teachers corrupt themselves, showing the penalty is self-inflicted, not sent from God.
In New Testament times the Dead Sea, where Sodom stood, was called the Lake of Fire, still smoking with burning sulphur, and people assumed it would smolder forever.
jude.differs: The topic reads strange flesh as forbidden contact with angels. Myers similarly links it to the angels but stresses Sodom's inhospitality and attempted rape of them, and he connects Jude's fire to the abuse of grace.

quote.text: It is not true grace if it cannot be abused.

lostparables.title: Which son is the true Prodigal Son in Luke 15:11-32?
lostparables.summary: Myers, who admits he often feels like the older son, argues both sons are prodigals: the younger lost in sin, the elder lost in the far country of religion and self-righteousness. The sequence of one in a hundred, one in ten and one in two leads to an unspoken fourth parable of the one: the reader. The story has no ending because we are invited to finish it. The father offers both sons the same unconditional love.
points: Asking for the inheritance was like wishing the father dead, yet the father effectively says he will die for his son. Landowners did not run; running was for servants.
The son is forgiven before he confesses. Forgiveness does not follow confession but precedes it.
Like the book of Jonah, the parable has no ending. We never learn whether the older son enters the party, because the reader must supply the answer.
The older son echoes Cain, who killed Abel out of anger at God accepting his brother. Abel's blood cried for vengeance; Jesus' blood speaks a better word of forgiveness.
Parties come only when a son realizes how badly he has failed and how much the father loves him. Death always precedes resurrection.
The faithful older son gets something special: the father says 'you are always with me.' Years of shared life and fellowship are worth more than any party.
lostparables.differs: The topic notes the elder brother mirrors the Pharisees and is left outside. Myers says there is ultimately no older son, only prodigals not yet awake, and pictures even reluctant elder brothers welcomed to a party at the end.

quote.text: We are just prodigal sons who have not yet woken up in the pig sty.

lostparables.title: What is the meaning of Luke 15 and the Lost Sheep, Lost Coin, and Prodigal Son?
lostparables.summary: Myers argues the three parables of Luke 15 are not about unbelievers becoming Christians but about straying believers being restored to fellowship with God. The sheep, coin and son already belonged to the shepherd, woman and father. He warns that reading the lost as all unbelievers can lead to universalism, since the shepherd searches until he has all one hundred. For him the chapter is an encouragement: God searches for those who stray and runs to welcome them home.
points: The shepherd does not add a new sheep to his fold; he recovers one that was already his. The same is true of the coin and the son.
Luke is a discipleship book, not an evangelistic one. It says little about receiving eternal life, which John's Gospel repeatedly says comes by believing in Jesus.
Myers cites an online conversation with a man who reached universalism partly by reading the lost as unbelievers, expecting the Shepherd found every last one of a lost world.
When God sees a straying believer far off, he does not make them crawl back and beg for forgiveness but runs with open arms and throws a party.
lostparables.differs: The topic presents universalists, annihilationists and traditionalists debating whether every lost one is found. Myers sidesteps that debate by limiting the lost to straying believers, and he cautions against the universalist reading.

quote.text: He will search high and low. He will scour every nook and cranny. He will never stop watching, waiting, and looking.

talents.title: The Parable of the Talents Revisited
talents.summary: Myers, who long taught the usual reading, now argues it is the opposite of what Jesus meant. In an honor-shame culture with a zero-sum economy, servants who multiplied money had taken it from others, which was shameful. The master is not Jesus but the god of this age, and the third servant, content with what he had, is the hero. Jesus is showing what his followers can expect from the world when they live by his code of honor.
points: Honor-shame cultures valued honor over wealth. The wealthy gained honor by giving back as patrons, funding music, arts, schools and hospitals.
The third servant would not even bank his talent to collect interest, read usury. The master shames him by taking what he has and giving it to the rich.
The words 'the kingdom of heaven is' in Matthew 25:14 are italicized in many Bibles because translators added them; the middle parable may contrast with those around it.
The master goes into a far country, the same place the prodigal son went, which represents life apart from fellowship with God.
Luke places the parable right after Zacchaeus, whom Jesus told to give away wealth gained from the poor rather than praising him as a good steward.
The master's demand to slay his enemies foreshadows Jesus' own death. Jesus then heads to Jerusalem and clears the temple of those enriching themselves by robbing the poor.
talents.differs: The topic treats the master as the returning king and sees Archelaus behind Luke's nobleman. Myers says the master cannot represent Jesus at all: he is the god of this age, and the fearful servant is the hero.

quote.text: The hero of the story if the third servant, who did not become richer, but instead was content with what he was given.

objjustice.title: More Reasons Why God Does Not Punish Sin
objjustice.summary: Myers argues that God disciplines and judges but never punishes sin. In Jesus the sin issue has been completely dealt with, so God is not waiting on his throne to strike. Sin grieves God not because he hates it but because he loves us and knows how it hurts us. The pain we suffer is sin's natural consequence, not inflicted punishment: sin is its own punishment. He draws a practical lesson: stop punishing others and forgive as God does.
points: The picture of an angry God hurling lightning bolts at sinners comes from Greek mythology and Zeus, not from the God revealed in Jesus Christ.
Texts some English translations render as punishment are better translated as judgment, which can be positive or negative.
God saw our sin coming from billions of years away and still sent Jesus. Human sin is a tiny speck of sand in the ocean of his loving-kindness.
Sin is serious because it enslaves families, destroys lives and ruins relationships. Like a loving parent, God grieves that his children suffer.
Since it is glorious to overlook an offense, as Proverbs 19:11 says, believers should overlook, forgive, and trust the Holy Spirit to convict others.
objjustice.differs: The topic weighs whether retribution should be proportionate or restorative. Myers goes further: God does not punish at all, because sin carries its own punishment.

quote.text: Sin grieves God, not because of how much He hates sin, but because of How much He loves us.
